title: The rains retreat again

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sermon heard again, each truth with its own job. Your line was the wheel turns. When something hard came up, which job did it need? Day one thousand four hundred sixteen.

A monk has just promised to stay put for the whole rainy season. Then a message comes. A lay family who supports the monastery wants him to come and bless a new house, a few days' walk away. Or worse: his mother is ill. Does he go? Does the promise mean he has to stay inside the monastery walls no matter what? The monks in the Buddha's time asked exactly this kind of question, and the answers are in the monastic rule. You've met the rains retreat before, and how it began with complaints about trampled crops. Today, look at the promise itself, what it holds, and where it bends.
screen: `A PROMISE TO STAY PUT.` → `THEN A MESSAGE COMES.` → `WHERE DOES IT BEND?`

segments.voice: First, the promise. At the start of the rains, each monk settles into one dwelling and declares that he will spend the rains retreat there. In Pali the season is vassa, the rains. It isn't a vow of silence or a lockdown. It's a vow of place. Second, the bend. The monastic rule, in the section on entering the rains, allows a monk to leave for a short business, up to seven days, and return. When? If he's sent for by a lay supporter who wants to give a gift or hear the teaching. If a fellow monk or nun is sick and needs help. If his mother or father is ill. The rule is careful: he goes, he does what's needed, he comes back inside the time. So the retreat isn't a wall against people. It's a home base you return to. Third, why staying matters. Wandering is good for meeting people. Staying is good for going deep. In one place for a season, the same path to the same well, the same room, the same faces, there's less to plan and more room to practice. By custom, a monk's seniority is even counted in rains. Fourth, the lay side. In Theravada lands, some lay people take on a practice for the season too: keeping extra precepts on moon days, giving something up, or going to the temple more often. Not a season in a monastery, just one thing, kept in one place, all season long. That's today's invitation.
screen: `A VOW OF PLACE.` · `LEAVE FOR NEED, THEN RETURN.` · `STAYING LETS IT GO DEEP.` · then, large: `STAY IN ONE PLACE.`

segments.voice: Let's settle on this season's practice, if you'd like. Sit, and let the body settle. Feel where you're sitting: the floor, the chair, the room around you. This is a place you could return to. Now bring back the one practice you chose a few days ago, when the block on practice traditions closed. Ask: could I keep this one thing for the season, here, in this place? Not perfectly. Just keep coming back, the way a monk comes back inside the seven days. If it feels too big, make it smaller until it fits. Then rest in the place itself, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
The rains retreat. Vassa, the season when monks stay in one place, leaving only briefly for real need. Today's word.
Your line: stay in one place. Today, pick the spot where you'll do your practice this season, and do it there once. Day one thousand four hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries monks enter the rains retreat after the Asalha full moon, each declaring a dwelling for the season; some lay people take on extra precepts or give something up for the same months.

original.note: Pali vassa: the rains, the rainy season; the retreat is named for it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rains retreat is monks staying indoors during bad weather.

what a scholar hears: the seven-day business (sattahakaraniya) allowances in the Vinaya's section on entering the rains.
